doc.title: John Altman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 14, 2023

title: Funny Bones recording car crash in Los Angeles
summary: A chaotic Los Angeles session with a PAL video misunderstanding, missing equipment and sobbing engineers, yet the music synced.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Thank you, George. Over here we have a term called train wrecks where things just go really badly. Is there anything that pops into your head?

Oh God, not half. So we were doing a film, “Funny Bones” which is a wonderful comedy with Jerry Lewis and Oliver Platt and Lee Evans and Leslie Caron. And I had written basically an orchestral score with two percussionists. And I had in mind the sound of Weather Report for the rhythm. So I booked Alex Acuna and Michael Fisher in Los Angeles. And we couldn’t find the studio and we finally found one because we were ringing them up and saying, “Are you able to show PAL videos?” PAL videos of course were British standard, not NTSC pneumatics but PAL. And everyone said, “Sorry, no we can’t do it, sorry.” One studio said, “Yeah, no problem.” So we showed up at the studio and the first thing, the truck — it was in the basement. The truck with all the percussion couldn’t get into the car park. That was the start. They started unloading stuff and the studio was locked. So it all had to pile up in the car park. Then the guy turned up, not the engineer but the guy who ran the studio turned up and he had a baseball cap on backwards, which I thought oh this is not going to go well. Finally we got in and they couldn’t — they’d never recorded a live instrument. They’d only plugged in guitars into the desk. So they couldn’t get the microphone lead to stretch into the studio to clip on to the microphone to get it recorded. Then we found out that, “Have you got a PAL video” the guy thought he’d said “Have you got a video, pal?” And of course there wasn’t a PAL video in sight so we couldn’t look at the film. So the whole first session was attempting to stretch a lead to the microphone into the room with no picture whatsoever. And at one point I went outside and the engineer, a very famous movie soundtrack engineer, and my producer were on — they had their heads on adjacent wheelie bins sobbing, literally in tears. I went back in and the director was sitting in the back of me and he went, “It’s all going terribly well.” Somehow we persuaded them to stay for another three hours and we actually got it going. And there was no orchestral track obviously, this is pre the orchestra. And I had my timings. So they recorded to my timings. Then we got ready to take the tape back to London and the guy in the studio said, “You’ve got a problem here because they haven’t given you enough run-up to synchronize the music to the film.” So my producer on the last day when we were due to fly back to England and had a rush to a film facility where they inserted blank tape into the recording. And we got back to London thinking well tough, we’ve blown the whole thing. And it worked. Everything fitted. But that was just about the — that was the car crash. That was the car crash session.
